Bedlington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south-east Northumberland
s1loc: Bedlington gives its name to the Bedlington terrier, the lamb-like breed first bred here in the early 1800s, and the town wears that heritage proudly along its broad Front Street market town spine. Bedlington Country Park, a 57-hectare Local Nature Reserve on the wooded banks of the River Blyth, traces the old Bedlington Iron Works of Michael Longridge that built locomotives for Holland and Italy, making the valley the town's marquee draw.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Gallagher Park, laid out over the old Doctor Pit colliery, where a coal truck marks the mine shaft above football pitches, a BMX track and the red and black Noel and Liam mountain-bike trails. Doctor Pit Park, Humford Mill and the riverside paths along the Blyth Dene give activity and outdoor operators a varied offer, with the Northumberland coast a short run east.

Heritage and culture run through St Cuthbert's Church, where the saint's body is said to have rested, and the Monks of Newminster who first worked coal and coppiced the Blyth valley centuries ago. The annual Bedlington Terrier Show and the town's Pit and Plough mining past colour the events calendar, with the Bedlingtonshire heritage and the historic Salvin's Bridge anchoring a proper market-town character.

The visitor trade leans on the wider south-east Northumberland base, with guest houses, inns and the day-trip draw of Blyth's beach and Spine Road. Bedlington sits on the A1068 corridor close to the reopened Northumberland Line rail link to Newcastle, and the surrounding pull of Blyth, Cramlington and Ashington, plus Druridge Bay and Woodhorn beyond, feeds a steady seasonal flow into the town.

Morpeth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Northumberland
s1loc: Morpeth sits in a loop of the River Wansbeck as the historic county town of Northumberland, its skyline marked by the rare 17th-century Clock Tower on Oldgate, raised from recycled Newminster Abbey stone with six bells cast in 1706 by Richard Phelps. The 13th-century Morpeth Chantry on the bridge and the surviving gatehouse of Morpeth Castle, above its scheduled motte and bailey in Carlisle Park, anchor the town's marquee draws.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Carlisle Park, an award-winning green space with riverside rowing on the Wansbeck, tennis courts, a paddling pool, an aviary and one of only four working floral clocks in the UK. The William Turner Garden honours the Morpeth-born Father of English Botany, while the wooded paths up to Ha' Hill and the ruins of Newminster Abbey give walkers and activity operators a year-round seasonal offer.

Heritage and culture run through the Morpeth Chantry Bagpipe Museum, home to more than 120 sets of pipes including Northumbrian smallpipes from the W A Cocks collection and a set linked to King Louis XIV. The Northern Poetry Library and Craft Centre share the Chantry, the Sanderson Arcade brings a smart shopping run, and the Morpeth Northumbrian Gathering fills a busy local events calendar.

The visitor trade rests on town-centre hotels and guest houses, with guides leading castle, abbey and piping-heritage walks along the Wansbeck. Morpeth railway station on the East Coast Main Line and the A1 carry day-trippers in from Newcastle and beyond, and the surrounding draws of Ashington, Bedlington and Cramlington, plus Wallington and the Northumberland coast, feed a steady seasonal flow into the county town.

Hessle.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Humber shore
s1loc: Hessle sits beneath the iconic Humber Bridge, a 2,220-metre single-span suspension bridge opened in 1981 that towers over the foreshore as the town's signature landmark and the marquee draw for day-trippers along the Humber estuary. The Hessle Foreshore, with its slipway, playground and panoramic estuary views, and the surviving Black Mill, a five-sailed Scheduled Ancient Monument from the old chalk-quarrying trade, anchor the town's riverside visitor appeal.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Humber Bridge Country Park, a Local Nature Reserve opened in 1986 across the wooded chalk terraces of the old quarry, with the meadow, cliff and pond trails, a bird-feeding station and Little Switzerland below the cliffs. Over twenty butterfly species and great crested newts draw nature operators, while the Country Park Inn and the foreshore play park keep families busy through the season.

Heritage and culture run through All Saints' Church in the old village, the Hessle Square conservation area and a quarrying past stretching back to the 13th century when chalk was burned for whiting under the Black Mill. The TransPennine Trail and the Hessle Whiting Mill restoration project carry the town's industrial story, set against the wider draws of nearby Hull, the 2017 UK City of Culture.

The visitor trade leans on the deep Hull hotel base a few miles east and guest houses around Hessle, with guides running Humber Bridge and estuary walks. Hessle railway station on the Hull-to-Doncaster line and the A63 carry visitors in, and the surrounding pull of Hull, Cottingham and Beverley, with The Deep aquarium and Beverley Minster nearby, feeds a strong seasonal flow into the town.

Selby.region: Selby and the Vale of York
Selby.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Vale of York
s1loc: Selby is a historic market town on the River Ouse, dominated by Selby Abbey, a masterpiece of Gothic architecture founded in 1069 as the first abbey raised in the north of England after the Norman Conquest. Its great organ, soaring nave and the 14th-century Washington Window, whose heraldic shield is thought to have inspired the American flag, make the Abbey the town's outstanding marquee draw across the year.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Selby Park, five acres of green space in the heart of town with a pavilion, mini golf and legendary local ice cream, alongside the Selby Canal, opened in 1778, where narrowboats glide and visitors can take to the calm water. Skipwith Common National Nature Reserve and the riverside towpaths give walkers, cyclists and activity operators a varied seasonal offer in the surrounding Vale.

Heritage and culture run through Selby Town Hall, an intimate arts venue inside a 150-year-old former Primitive Methodist chapel with a strong touring programme, and the historic streets and weekly Monday market around the Abbey. Nearby Cawood Castle, the surviving gatehouse of the Archbishops of York's palace, the Selby Food and Drink Festival and the St Wilfrid's Day Parade in July fill a busy local events calendar.

The visitor trade rests on inns and guest houses across the town, with guides leading Abbey and waterway walks along the Ouse. Selby railway station links to Leeds, Hull and York, and the A19 and A63 carry day-trippers in, while the surrounding draws of Goole, York and Pontefract, plus the York Designer Outlet and the Drax visitor trade, feed a steady seasonal flow into the town.

Knaresborough.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Nidd Gorge
s1loc: Knaresborough is one of Yorkshire's most photographed towns, its houses tumbling down the gorge above the River Nidd beneath the 78-foot railway viaduct, completed in 1851 across the river as a masterpiece of Victorian engineering. The clifftop ruins of Knaresborough Castle, dating mostly from the early 14th century, with its King's Tower and the adjoining Courthouse Museum, give the town a commanding marquee draw above the Waterside.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Mother Shipton's Cave and the Petrifying Well, billed as England's oldest visitor attraction charging admission since 1630, set in ancient riverside woodland and the birthplace of the prophetess Ursula Sontheil. Rowing boats on the Nidd from Blenkhorn's boatyard, the riverside Waterside, and the three-mile Nidd Gorge walk to Grimbald Bridge give activity operators a strong year-round offer.

Heritage and culture run through the 1408 cliffside Chapel of Our Lady of the Crag, the cobbled Market Place with one of England's oldest chemist shops, and the eccentric Bebra Gardens below the castle. Conyngham Hall grounds, the FEVA festival of entertainment and visual arts, and the famous Bed Race down the gorge each June fill a lively events calendar in this Harrogate-district town.

The visitor trade rests on inns, guest houses and riverside cafes across the town, with guides leading castle, viaduct and Mother Shipton walks along the Nidd. Knaresborough railway station on the Harrogate line and the A59 carry day-trippers in, and the surrounding draws of Harrogate, Ripon and York, plus the spa town and Ripon Cathedral nearby, feed a strong seasonal flow into the gorge.

Clitheroe.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Ribble Valley
s1loc: Clitheroe is the gateway to the Ribble Valley, crowned by Clitheroe Castle, a late-12th-century Norman fortress raised by Robert de Lacy whose surviving keep is said to be the second smallest in England. Set in 16 acres of parkland, the keep gives sweeping views to Pendle Hill and the Forest of Bowland, while the Clitheroe Castle Museum below tells the town's history through an Edwardian kitchen and local geology displays as the marquee draw.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Castle grounds, home to Lancashire's first labyrinth, a bandstand, bowling green, war memorial and a skate park, with a Creative Activity Area at the foot of the keep. Riverside walks along the Ribble, the open moorland of Pendle Hill of witch-trial fame, and the trails of the Forest of Bowland Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty give walkers and outdoor operators a rich seasonal offer.

Heritage and culture run through Holmes Mill, a former textile mill reborn as a beer hall, food hall, cinema and hotel, and the bustling Clitheroe Market and independent shops along Castle Street and Moor Lane. The town's links to the 1612 Pendle Witch Trials, the Clitheroe Food Festival and the Great Days Out events colour a busy calendar across the Ribble Valley borough.

The visitor trade rests on inns, hotels and guest houses across town and the wider valley, with guides leading castle, Pendle and Bowland walks. Clitheroe railway station on the Ribble Valley Line and the A59 carry day-trippers in from Lancashire and beyond, and the surrounding draws of Burnley, Blackburn and Accrington, plus Whalley Abbey and Stonyhurst nearby, feed a steady seasonal flow into the town.

Neston.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Dee estuary
s1loc: Neston is a historic market town on the Wirral side of the Dee estuary, its marquee draw the nearby Ness Botanic Gardens, more than 60 acres of landscaped grounds founded by the cotton merchant Arthur Bulley, with rhododendrons, a rock garden and sweeping views across the estuary to the Welsh hills. The old port of Parkgate, once busier than Liverpool before the Dee silted up, draws visitors to its seafront and famous shrimps along The Parade.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Wirral Country Park, Britain's first designated country park, opened in 1973 along the Wirral Way over the trackbed of the old Hooton-to-West Kirby railway that once served Neston Colliery. The Burton Marsh boardwalk along the Dee, the Thurstaston visitor centre and miles of estuary cycling and birdwatching at the RSPB Parkgate marshes give activity operators a strong seasonal offer.

Heritage and culture run through St Mary and St Helen's Church with its rare Viking-age cross fragments, the Neston Cross and the town's old colliery and salt-trade past, recalled at Hadlow Road station preserved in Edwardian dress. The Neston Female Friendly Society's Ladies' Day procession, one of Britain's oldest, and the cobbled streets of Burton village nearby colour a distinctive local calendar.

The visitor trade rests on inns and guest houses across Neston and Parkgate, with guides leading estuary, marsh and Wirral Way walks. Neston railway station on the Borderlands line and the A540 carry day-trippers in from Chester and Merseyside, and the surrounding draws of Bromborough, Heswall and Ellesmere Port, plus Port Sunlight and the National Waterways Museum, feed a steady seasonal flow into the town.
